card werk-client-reload  [open]
In dev, Vite runs inside the werk server, and a client change it cannot apply in place reloads the page
why: #werk-dev was decided for a client with no build step. With a Vite client (#werk-stack), the server must transform the client itself, and the reload rule must still keep the draft.

In dev, the werk server runs Vite inside its own process to transform the React client, so there is one process and one port, and the server's lock and hot-reload guard (#werk-hmr) still cover everything. A client change that Vite applies in place needs no reload. A change it cannot apply in place sends the reload event on the live channel that #werk-dev decides, and the composer draft survives it in session storage, as #werk-dev requires. Each tab's draft is kept by tab (#werk-mc-follow).

  -> refines         werk  werk v0
for i in werk-dev werk-hmr werk-stack werk-mc-follow; do node src/cli.ts show $i | head -12; echo ---; done

card werk-dev  [decided]
npm run dev: hot-reload src, reload the page on web
why: Without it, a code change needs a manual restart and a manual refresh: two steps between an edit and seeing it.
subtree: 2 cards, 2 decided

`npm run dev` runs `werk serve` under `bun --hot`. A change under src/ reloads the changed module in the same process, so a live chat session survives it. #werk-hmr decides the runtime and the guard that keeps the server from starting twice. Bun does not watch web/, because the server never imports those files.

web/ is handled in the server. A change there pushes a `reload` event on the same SSE stream the map already listens to, and the page reloads itself. A `changed` event only refetches the graph, which is not enough: the browser is still running the old page code.

The draft in the composer is stashed in the browser's session storage before the reload and restored after it. The open card is in the hash and the transcript is on the server, so nothing else lives in the page.

Two races remain for a full restart, when a new process starts before the old one has died:
---
card werk-hmr  [decided]
Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits
why: Research, two rounds of real-app testing, and a direct repro of the one open correctness concern settle it. Two priorities settle the rest: productionization and upgrade risk. See #werk-hmr:src0 through src5, and options opt1/opt2.

The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

Research (#werk-hmr:src0): vite-node invalidates transitively, not globally. Bun --hot guarantees the global object survives. Deno --watch-hmr names an in-flight async function as a forced-full-restart case, the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR.

Toy prototype (#werk-hmr:src1): a minimal harness shaped like werk's agent, pinned on the global object, survived edits to both a sibling module and the pinned module itself, under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch.

Real-app test, unpatched (#werk-hmr:src2): werk's real code has neither guard. vite-node --watch crashed outright on an unrelated-file edit (an EADDRINUSE retry loop, then exit code 1). bun --hot did not crash, but silently orphaned a live task on the same edit.

---
card werk-stack  [decided]
The frontend needs a component stack
why: The current frontend is 2422 lines of hand-rolled rendering. Two choices decide the replacement, each on its own card below.
subtree: 4 cards, 4 decided, 1 unchallenged

A new implementation is built on this stack from scratch — this card is not a migration plan, and nothing here asks anyone to port the current frontend.

Two separate choices, each decided on its own card:

    framework    React + Vite              #werk-stack-framework
    hydration    islands as a pattern      #werk-stack-hydration

---
card werk-mc-follow  [decided]
The conversation owns the card. The map follows the focused tab.
why: The scope shown above the composer must be the tab's card, not the previous tab's. So the map must move.
subtree: 2 cards, 2 decided

The conversation owns the card, and the map follows it. The arrow points from the tab to the map, not from the map to the tab.

Without tabs, the map owns the position and the scope chip above the composer reflects it: map -> chip. Tabs invert it. The conversation owns its card; focusing a tab sets both the chip and the main view: tab -> (chip, map).

Why it is not cosmetic. Every turn starts with '[the map is now at #id]'. A tab resumed while the map still shows the previous tab's card would be told the wrong subject, and it would follow it. The conversation would change topic without either of you deciding to.

card kill-shape  [decided]
A criterion has a source, metric, threshold, and window, or a stated reason for none
why: Without all four parts an agent cannot check the criterion. Without a stated reason, a missing metric hides an unclear hypothesis.

Machine-checkable form: data source, metric, threshold, time window, minimum sample size. The agent drafts the query. The author confirms it.

No-metric reasons and their revisit mechanism:

| Reason | Meaning | Revisit |
|---|---|---|
| Unclear hypothesis | Cannot say why this beat the alternatives | Agent pushes back once |
| Not worth measuring | Cheap and reversible (copy, spacing) | Not tracked |
| Slow or noisy | Real effect outside the feedback window (trust, retention) | Proxy metric and a review date |
| Taste or values | A commitment, not a hypothesis | Link to a written principle |
| Constraint | Regulatory or contractual | Event trigger on the source |
| Manual test | The author checks it by use | Review date, or the next use |

The warning sign is a decision with no stated reason, not a decision with no metric.

  -> refines         kill  Every decision carries kill criteria: what must become true to revisit it

  <- depends_on      kill-ask  The agent asks for kill criteria on an open card. The CLI blocks decided until they are recorded
  <- depends_on      kill-render  Kill criteria render as a section right below the card, one row per criterion

card st-build-ticket-order  [decided]
A builder pass: checks stop at the first red, then the grader, then the review
why: The cheap verdict runs first. A grader or reviewer that breaks must not let a pass through.

1. The checks run in order and stop at the first red one.
2. The grader runs only on green checks. It scores the decided cards of the ticket's depends_on closure (#lp-prod-judge); a card it leaves out scores 0.
3. The five reviewers run only on a passing grade. An unknown severity counts as MEDIUM and does not block.
4. A broken or silent grader or reviewer fails the pass as a failed step, with the reason in the next brief.

A silenced builder pass still commits its edits, skips the checks, and counts against the cap. A ticket whose build ends red stays in building. Each build writes one card obligation (#st-build-card); an unsatisfied obligation does not block the build.

  -> refines         st-build-ticket  The builder loop: one ticket, fresh passes until the checks, the grader, and the review pass
  -> depends_on      lp-prod-judge  The production judgements

  -> depends_on      lp-prod-review  The quality review
       why: The pass runs the five reviewers and treats severities by the quality review rules of #lp-prod-review.
  -> depends_on      st-build-silence-act  On silence, the overseer cancels the session and a fresh pass starts

card st-build-ticket  [decided]
The builder loop: one ticket, fresh passes until the checks, the grader, and the review pass
why: A fix is a new implement pass with the failure in its input, so the loop has no separate fix step.
subtree: 3 cards, 3 decided

One ticket, one worktree.

1. Implement. A fresh builder agent does one unit of work toward the ticket (#st-build-implement).
2. Check. The checks run: one command each, exit code only (#lp-checks).
3. Grade. A grader agent reads the diff against each decided card (#lp-prod-judge).
4. Review. Five reviewer agents, one per quality area, read the diff (#lp-prod-review).

A fail at step 2, 3, or 4 starts a new pass at step 1. There is no separate fix step. A retry cap stops the loop (default 5; #st-build-run-mechanics).

#st-build-ticket-order gives the order inside one pass.

card st-ticket-set-checks  [decided]
Three checks on the whole ticket set: cards cited, stories delivered, blocked_by
why: Coverage and order are properties of the set. No single ticket can pass or fail them alone.

The set checks read the tickets of one plan run that passed their own checks (#st-ticket-own-checks), the decided cards of the planned subtree, the depends_on edges between those cards, and the spec's story numbers. A ticket that fails its own checks is not on the board, so its cites and stories do not count.

**1. Cards cited.** Every decided card in the planned subtree is in the `cites:` of at least one ticket. A failure lists the cards no ticket cites.

**2. Stories delivered.** Every story number in the spec is in the `stories:` of at least one ticket (#st-ticket-stories). No ticket lists a number that is not in the spec. A failure lists the missing or unknown numbers.

**3. blocked_by.** Three conditions:
- Every number in `blocked_by` is a ticket in the set. A blocker that failed its own checks is not in the set, so it fails this condition.
- The `blocked_by` graph has no cycle.
- It agrees with depends_on. For each depends_on edge A → B between two subtree cards, every ticket that cites A either also cites B, or is blocked_by every ticket that cites B. An edge to a card that no ticket cites is left to check 1.
